rv.q: It's a richly thoughtful piece, and with it Steiner joins an august list of playwrights — Beckett, Pinter, Churchill, Crimp — who have deliberately limited their own currency or undermined dramatic structure to talk about the absurdities and inequities of life.
Yet a vital sense of disturbance is almost entirely absent.
'Lemons Lemons Lemons Lemons Lemons' is still good after its richly deserved West End glow-up, it's just that it's gone a little sour.
I found the evening twee, contrived and implausible - a bit of a lemon, in fact.
The staging is pseudish, the plotting episodic and the script bland for a play about the value of language.
Jenna Coleman and Aidan Turner work wonderfully well together, bouncing off each other, both in moments of levity and solemnity.
Coleman and Turner are a powerfully charismatic double act.
Lemons forces the audience to contemplate the horror of a wordless life, but outstays its welcome.
The rather cool perfection of the production works less well than fringe versions of the play, whose intimacy gives it a more powerful sense of life.
Overall, sadly, it is a bit of a lemon.
The thing is harmless enough but impossible to get fired up about.
